answers.summary: Ventura County's base property tax is 1% of assessed value. Voter-approved bonds bring the total to about 1.04% to 1.23%, depending on city and tax rate area. Thousand Oaks and Moorpark are at the low end and Oxnard is at the high end. Fixed direct assessments and any Mello-Roos taxes are added on top.
answers.answer:
### FY 2025-26 ad valorem rates by city (Auditor-Controller Tax Rate Book)
| City | Most common TRA rate | Range seen |
|---|---|---|
| Thousand Oaks | 1.0480% | 1.0410%–1.1719% |
| Moorpark | 1.0722% | 1.0480%–1.0722% |
| Ojai | 1.0866% (one TRA sampled) | n/a |
| Ventura | 1.0880% (also 1.0920%) | 1.0880%–1.1742% |
| Simi Valley | 1.0956% | 1.0886%–1.0956% |
| Camarillo | 1.1056% | 1.0917%–1.1520% |
| Santa Paula | 1.1065% / 1.1269% | 1.0887%–1.1269% |
| Fillmore | 1.1473% | 1.1473% |
| Port Hueneme | 1.1547% (one TRA sampled) | n/a |
| Oxnard | **1.2318%** (also 1.1754%) | 1.0966%–1.2318% |

Each rate = **1.000% countywide (Prop 13)** plus that tax rate area's (TRA's) school, community college and water bond rates. Rates change a little every year as bond payments change.

### On top of the rate
- **Direct assessments**: flat or per-unit charges for things like sewer, lighting and landscaping districts, flood control, and vector control. They appear as separate lines on the bill and don't depend on price.
- **Mello-Roos (CFD) special taxes**: mostly in **newer master-planned subdivisions**, and rare on older apartment buildings. Always check the actual bill.

### Underwriting a purchase
Under Prop 13 the sale resets the assessed value to the price:

New tax ≈ price × TRA rate + direct assessments

Example: a **$6,000,000 Oxnard** building at 1.2318% is about **$73,900/yr** plus assessments. The same price in **Thousand Oaks** at 1.048% is about **$62,900**, roughly $11,000/yr less. Assessed value can then rise no more than **2% per year**.

### So what
Never underwrite the seller's current tax bill. Re-run taxes at the purchase price using the parcel's TRA, and pull the actual bill to catch assessments and CFDs.
keyPoints: Base rate 1.000% plus voter-approved bonds: about 1.04%–1.23% total in Ventura County cities (FY 2025-26)
Lowest: Thousand Oaks (mostly 1.048%) and Moorpark (1.0722%); highest: Oxnard (up to 1.2318%)
A sale resets assessed value to the price; increases are then capped at 2% a year
Direct assessments and Mello-Roos are added on top; check the actual tax bill

answers.summary: Ventura County charges the standard documentary transfer tax of $1.10 per $1,000 of value, which is 0.11%. None of the county's cities add their own transfer tax. The seller customarily pays it, so a $5M sale costs about $5,500. That is a big advantage over the City of Los Angeles and its Measure ULA tiers.
answers.answer:
### The rate
- **County documentary transfer tax (DTT): $1.10 per $1,000** ($0.55 per $500) of value transferred. This is the standard rate under California's Documentary Transfer Tax Act. In cities, the county and city split it, with the city's half credited against the county tax, so the total stays $1.10.
- **City transfer taxes in Ventura County: none listed.** Chicago Title's **2026** customary practices guide shows only the county $1.10 for Ventura County. Santa Barbara County is the same.

### Who pays (custom, negotiable)
| Item | Ventura County custom |
|---|---|
| Escrow fees | Split buyer/seller |
| Owner's title policy | Seller |
| County DTT | Seller |

Commercial closings often split escrow 50/50, with the seller paying the standard-coverage title premium.

### Quick math
| Price | DTT at $1.10/$1,000 |
|---|---|
| $2,000,000 | $2,200 |
| $5,000,000 | $5,500 |
| $10,000,000 | $11,000 |

State law generally lets the tax exclude **liens or encumbrances remaining on the property at the time of sale**, such as an assumed loan. Confirm that with escrow on each deal.

### Compared with neighbors
- **City of Los Angeles (Measure ULA)**: $4.50/$1,000 below $5.4M, then **4%** from $5.4M to $10.9M and **5.5%** above $10.9M. A $6M LA sale owes about **$240,000** in city transfer tax, against **$6,600** for the same price in Ventura County.
- Santa Monica and Culver City also have steep tiered taxes.

### So what
For LA-based sellers and buyers, Ventura County's low transfer cost is a real selling point. It supports investors moving capital across the county line, especially exchange buyers leaving LA.
keyPoints: Ventura County DTT: $1.10 per $1,000 (0.11%); no additional city transfer taxes listed (2026)
Custom: seller pays DTT and owner's title policy; escrow fees split
$5M sale: about $5,500 DTT
City of LA ULA: 4% from $5.4M to $10.9M, 5.5% above (2026 guide)
Assumed loans may be excluded from the taxable value under state law; confirm with escrow

answers.summary: In a 1031 exchange the seller has 45 days from closing to identify replacement property in writing and 180 days to close, or by the tax-return due date if that comes first. Neither deadline is ever extended. A qualified intermediary must hold the cash. To defer all the tax, the seller has to buy equal or greater value and replace the debt.
answers.answer:
### The rules (IRC §1031)
- **Like-kind real property** held for investment or business use. Since 2018, **real property only**. Property held primarily for sale (flips, dealer property) doesn't qualify. Apartments can be exchanged for any investment real estate, anywhere in the U.S.
- **45 days**: identify replacement property in writing, delivered to the QI or the other party.
- **180 days**: close, or by the **tax-return due date, with extensions**, if that comes first.
- **Qualified intermediary (QI)**: the seller can't receive or control the sale proceeds. Pick the QI carefully; there have been QI failures.
- **Identification rules** (Treasury regs): up to **3 properties** of any value, or any number if their total is ≤**200%** of the relinquished value, or more than that if you buy **95%** of what you identified.
- **Related parties**: if either side sells within **2 years**, the deferral is lost.

### Full deferral checklist
1. Buy **equal or greater value**.
2. Reinvest **all net equity**.
3. **Replace the debt** paid off, with new debt or added cash.

Any cash out or debt reduction is taxable "**boot**."

### Common pitfalls
- **Missing the 45-day deadline** with no backup properties. Many sellers identify a DST as a backup (Q173).
- **Sales late in the year**: if the client files on April 15, the 180 days get cut short. File an extension.
- **Same taxpayer**: the entity that sells must buy, so partnership splits need early planning ("drop and swap").
- **Paying non-exchange costs from proceeds** (loan fees, prorations) creates boot.
- **California clawback**: if CA property is exchanged for out-of-state property, the seller files **FTB Form 3840 every year**, and California taxes the deferred gain when the replacement is eventually sold.

### So what
Line up replacement candidates **before** listing. In tight markets, the 45-day clock, not the buyer, is what kills an exchange.

*Educational only, not tax advice. Have the client confirm with their CPA or tax attorney.*
keyPoints: 45 days to identify, 180 days (or the tax-return due date, if earlier) to close; no extensions
Real property only since 2018; held for investment or business use
Full deferral: equal or greater value, all equity reinvested, debt replaced; anything else is boot
ID rules: 3-property, 200%, or 95%
CA to out-of-state exchanges: annual FTB Form 3840; California taxes the deferred gain later

answers.summary: A Delaware Statutory Trust (DST) is a sponsor-packaged, fractional, passive ownership interest that the IRS treats as like-kind real estate for a 1031 exchange (Rev. Rul. 2004-86). Older Ventura County sellers often use DSTs as a backup identification or to retire from management, though I found no local data on how often.
answers.answer:
### What a DST is
- A trust holds one or more properties, usually with **non-recourse debt already in place**. Investors buy **fractional beneficial interests**.
- **Rev. Rul. 2004-86**: the IRS treats a properly structured DST as an investment trust, so an interest counts as like-kind replacement property.
- The trust has to stay passive. The trustee **can't** raise new capital, renegotiate the loan, sign new leases (except on tenant bankruptcy), buy or swap properties, or make more than minor non-structural changes.

### Why sellers use them
- **No management**: an exit from tenants, toilets and rent-control paperwork.
- **Deadline insurance**: DSTs can be identified on day 44 and closed fast. Many exchangers list one as a **backup** inside the 45 days.
- **Matching value and debt**: buy any amount to fill the "equal or greater" and debt-replacement tests.
- **Diversification** across regions and property types, and smaller pieces that can go to different heirs.
- **Estate plan**: hold until death for a stepped-up basis (Q177). Some sponsors offer a later **721 UPREIT** rollup (Q174).

### Trade-offs to explain
- **Illiquid**, with no control over when the property sells, often a 5–10 year hold.
- **Sponsor fees and loads**, so returns are lower than owning directly. Read the private placement memorandum.
- Usually limited to **accredited investors**.
- The trustee can't fix problems, such as refinancing a maturing loan. Some DSTs have struggled for that reason.
- Some lenders exclude DSTs as borrowers. For example, Freddie's Conventional Small lists DSTs as ineligible.

### How common in Ventura County?
I found **no published data**. Long-held, high-basis-gain owners near retirement, a common Ventura County profile, are the usual DST buyers. Inventory of good replacement properties is thin. Ask local QIs.

### So what
Raise the DST option early with retiring sellers. It can turn "I'd sell but I don't want the tax" into a listing.

*Educational only, not tax advice. Have the client confirm with their CPA or tax attorney.*
keyPoints: DST interests qualify as 1031 replacement property under Rev. Rul. 2004-86
The trustee can't raise capital, refinance, re-lease (except on tenant bankruptcy) or swap properties
Uses: backup identification, exact value and debt matching, passive retirement, estate planning
Trade-offs: illiquid, sponsor fees, no control, generally accredited investors only
No published Ventura County usage data

answers.summary: There are three other ways to defer or spread the tax. An installment sale spreads the gain over the years the buyer pays. A 721 UPREIT swaps the building for REIT operating-partnership units, tax-deferred, often after a 1031 into a DST. A charitable remainder trust (CRT) sells the property without immediate tax and pays the owner income for life, but the remainder goes to charity.
answers.answer:
### Installment sale (seller carryback)
- Gain is reported **as principal is received**, which spreads it across years.
- **Ordinary-income recapture is taxed in the year of sale**. This matters for cost-segregated personal property.
- Interest is ordinary income and must meet **AFR** minimums.
- Risk: the buyer's credit. Large deferred balances can also trigger an interest charge on the deferred tax.

### 721 UPREIT
- **IRC §721**: no gain is recognized when property is contributed to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest.
- The owner contributes the building to a REIT's **operating partnership** for **OP units**: diversified income, and the units still step up at death.
- **Converting OP units to REIT shares, or redeeming them, is taxable.** The owner also gives up control and future 1031 options.
- Common path: **1031 into a DST, then the sponsor rolls the DST into an UPREIT** a few years later.

### Charitable remainder trust (CRT)
- The owner gives the property to an **irrevocable** CRT. The trust sells without immediate tax and reinvests the full proceeds.
- Pays the owner **5%–50% a year**: a fixed amount (CRAT) or a percentage of trust value (CRUT).
- At least **10% of the initial value must go to charity**. The owner gets a partial charitable deduction up front.
- Payments are taxed in tiers: ordinary income, then capital gain, then other income, then tax-free return of principal.
- Trade-off: **heirs don't get the property**. Some owners buy life insurance to replace it.

### Which fits whom
| Goal | Tool |
|---|---|
| Wants income, trusts the buyer | Installment sale |
| Wants out of management, keep deferring | DST, then 721 |
| Charitable, wants lifetime income, no heirs or other assets for heirs | CRT |
| Wants to keep the property | Hold until death (Q177) |

### So what
These tools turn "I can't sell because of taxes" into a yes. Bring in the CPA early.

*Educational only, not tax advice. Have the client confirm with their CPA or tax attorney.*
keyPoints: Installment sale: gain taxed as principal is received; ordinary-income recapture taxed in the year of sale
§721: tax-free contribution to a partnership, used to get REIT OP units (UPREIT); converting units later is taxable
Common path: 1031 into a DST, then rollup into a 721 UPREIT
CRT: irrevocable; pays 5%–50% a year; at least 10% of initial value to charity; sells without immediate tax

answers.summary: Under the July 2025 law (OBBBA), 100% bonus depreciation is permanent for property acquired after January 19, 2025. A cost segregation study can move roughly a fifth to a third of an apartment building's basis into 5-, 7- and 15-year property and write it all off in year one. The big catches are passive-loss limits, California's non-conformity, and recapture when the owner sells.
answers.answer:
### The law (as of Oct 2026)
- **OBBBA (Pub. L. 119-21, signed July 4, 2025)** restored a **permanent 100%** additional first-year (bonus) depreciation for qualified property **acquired after January 19, 2025**, using the binding-contract date. Before that, the TCJA phase-down would have allowed **40%** in 2025.
- IRS **Notice 2026-11** gives interim guidance and allows an election to take 40% instead.
- **Section 179** limit for 2026: **$2,560,000**, phasing out above $4,090,000. Section 179 has limited use for residential rentals.

### How cost segregation works
The building itself (27.5-year straight-line) is split into components:
- **5/7-year**: appliances, carpet, cabinetry, some electrical
- **15-year**: paving, landscaping, site lighting, fences
Those components qualify for bonus depreciation. Land never depreciates.

### Worked example (assumptions)
**$6M purchase, 40% land**, so a **$3.6M** depreciable basis. Assume the study reclassifies **25%** ($900K).

| | Year-1 depreciation (approx.) |
|---|---|
| No cost seg | $3.6M ÷ 27.5 ≈ **$131K** |
| Cost seg + 100% bonus | $900K + ($2.7M ÷ 27.5) ≈ **$998K** |

(Ignores mid-month convention.)

### The catches
- **Passive-loss rules**: unless the investor is a qualifying **real estate professional**, losses mainly offset other passive income. Unused losses carry forward and are freed up on sale.
- **California generally doesn't follow federal bonus depreciation**, so state taxes still use regular depreciation.
- **Recapture**: on a taxable sale, the reclassified personal property is recaptured as **ordinary income**. A 1031 exchange can defer this, but exchanges involving personal property components need care.

### So what
For high-income buyers, especially real estate professionals, year-one tax savings can **boost the effective first-year return** and help justify a tight cap rate. Model it, but don't let it make up for a bad deal.

*Educational only, not tax advice. Have the client confirm with their CPA or tax attorney.*

IRS Notice 2026-11 is the interim §168(k) guidance

Example: $3.6M basis, 25% reclassified: year-1 depreciation ≈ $998K vs ≈ $131K
Catches: passive-loss limits, California non-conformity, ordinary-income recapture on sale

answers.summary: Take a building bought for $1.5M in 1996 that is fully depreciated and sells for $6M. The seller's combined federal and California tax is roughly $1.9M, about a third of the net proceeds. That is why 1031 exchanges and step-up planning drive so many Ventura County listing decisions.
answers.answer:
### The rates (2026)
- **Federal long-term capital gain**: 20% top rate (applies above **$613,700** taxable income for joint filers and **$545,500** for single filers in 2026).
- **Unrecaptured §1250 gain** (straight-line depreciation taken on the building): taxed at up to **25%**.
- **Net investment income tax (NIIT)**: **3.8%** for most passive owners.
- **California** taxes capital gains as **ordinary income**: top bracket **12.3%**, plus the **1% Mental Health Services Tax** on income over $1M, for a **13.3%** top rate. There is no lower capital-gains rate.

### Worked example (married couple, no other income; simplified)
| Step | Amount |
|---|---|
| Purchase 1996 (40% land) | $1,500,000 |
| Building basis ($900K) depreciated 27.5 yrs, now fully used | −$900,000 |
| **Adjusted basis** | **$600,000** |
| Sale price | $6,000,000 |
| Selling costs (3%) | −$180,000 |
| **Total gain** | **$5,220,000** |

| Tax | Calculation | Approx. |
|---|---|---|
| Unrecaptured §1250 | $900K × 25% | $225,000 |
| Federal LTCG | $4.32M × 20% | $864,000 |
| NIIT | $5.22M × 3.8% | $198,000 |
| California | 2025 Schedule Y on $5.22M ≈ $604K + 1% MHST on $4.22M | $646,000 |
| **Total** | | **≈ $1.93M** |

That is about **37% of the gain** and **33% of net proceeds**. Using top rates overstates it a little, because some gain falls in lower brackets. State tax is largely not deductible federally because of the SALT cap.

### Key insight
For a long hold, **capital improvements raise the basis**. Every dollar of depreciation the owner took comes back at **25% federal plus California ordinary rates**.

### So what
Show sellers a simple net sheet like this one early. It explains why many say "I'll never sell," and it opens the 1031, DST, installment sale, and hold-until-death conversations (Q172–Q177).

*Educational only, not tax advice. Have the client confirm with their CPA or tax attorney.*
keyPoints: 2026 federal 20% LTCG bracket starts at $613,700 (joint) / $545,500 (single)
Unrecaptured §1250 gain: up to 25%; NIIT 3.8%
California taxes gains as ordinary income: 12.3% top bracket plus 1% over $1M = 13.3%
Example: $6M sale, $600K adjusted basis: about $5.22M gain and about $1.93M total tax (~37% of gain)

answers.summary: At death, heirs get a stepped-up basis equal to fair market value, which wipes out both the capital gain and the depreciation recapture. In California community property, both halves step up at the first spouse's death. For an owner in their 80s, holding can save more than $1.9M of tax. The trade-offs are Prop 19 property-tax reassessment for heirs who keep the building, and the management burden in the meantime.
answers.answer:
### The rules
- **IRC §1014(a)(1)**: inherited property takes a basis equal to **fair market value at date of death**. The gain, and the depreciation recapture, disappear.
- **§1014(b)(6) community property**: the **surviving spouse's half also steps up**. For a California married couple holding as community property, the entire building can step up at the first death.
- **Federal estate tax**: the basic exclusion is **$15,000,000 per person in 2026** under OBBBA, indexed from 2027. That is about $30M for a married couple. Most Ventura County owners won't owe estate tax.

### Sell vs. hold: the Q176 building
| | Sell now at 85 | Hold until death; heirs sell at $6M |
|---|---|---|
| Basis | $600K | $6.0M (stepped up) |
| Tax on sale | **≈ $1.9M** | **≈ $0**, plus any appreciation after death |
| Net to family | ≈ $3.9M | ≈ $5.8M (after 3% costs) |

### The catches
- **Prop 19 (effective Feb 16, 2021)** **eliminated** the parent-child exclusion for property **other than a principal residence** (and family farms). An inherited apartment building is **reassessed to market value**. A Prop 13 base of perhaps **$2.7M** ($1.5M grown at 2%/yr for 30 years) could reset to **$6M**. At ~1.1%, that's about **$36K/yr** more property tax if heirs keep it. It doesn't matter if they sell.
- **Management and capital needs**: an aging owner may be letting the building slide. Deferred maintenance reduces the value the heirs inherit.
- **Middle paths**: a **1031 exchange into a DST** or NNN property, or a **721 UPREIT**, moves the owner out of management and *still* keeps the step-up at death ("swap till you drop").

### So what
With older owners, ask about their **estate plan and how title is held** before pushing a sale. Often the best listing is the one that helps the **heirs** after the step-up. Build those relationships early, and be the broker the trustee calls.

*Educational only, not tax advice. Have the client confirm with their CPA or tax attorney.*
